An Onmyōji is a practitioner of Onmyōdō, a form of magic associated with fortune-telling and divination. They were employed by the noble class to provide advice and guidance on matters such as battle plans, marriage prospects, political decisions, and more. Beyond their divination skills, Onmyōji were repositories of knowledge in areas such as Japanese folklore, astrological calendars, the philosophy of yin and yang, and the five elements.

Onmyōji were highly valued in the various courts of the shoguns and held considerable influence during the feudal period. Perhaps the most famous Onmyōji was Abe-no-Seimei (921–1005 CE), who lived during the Heian period.

historia: The shoguns were elite military rulers in feudal Japan. The term, which means 'commander of the army,' was first applied at the end of the Heian period. The first shogunate was formed by Minamoto no Yoritomo in 1192 CE, establishing the position of shogun as a hereditary military dictatorship until 1867 CE. The shoguns were only one step below the emperor, making them among the most powerful individuals in Japan. However, the shoguns eventually gained so much power that the emperor became merely a symbolic figurehead, while the true power rested with the shoguns.

The Asura is a three-faced, red skinned warrior demigod that originates from Buddhist traditions but was later incorporated into the Japanese mythological world through religious syncretism. Along with having three faces, the Asura also possesses six arms, each wielding six different weapons.

Asuras are known to have chaotic emotions, and they are typically driven by their base instincts: pride, violence, and greed. As beings of chaos and war, it is fitting that they are associated with fire – they hurl fireballs with several of their many arms to incinerate their enemies when provoked.

With a haunting, shrill voice, the Onmoraki is known to plague neglectful religious officials outside of shrines and temples. One of its most chilling talents is the ability to imitate the voice of the person that it is harassing, taunting them about their failures.

Some Japanese legends suggest that Onmorakis originate from recently deceased people with unsettled spirits – if a human dies without the correct burial practice, their spirit transforms into an Onmoraki.

Although Shinigamis appear human-like, their sunken, sallow skin and eerie features make it clear that these beings are demons from the afterlife. These death spirits haunt areas where people have recently died. Local legends across Japan suggest that acts of violence invite more violence – explaining the appearance of the Shinigami. Some stories claim that the Shinigami can possess people and drive them to commit violent acts.

A mysterious aquatic giant, the Umibōzu is a calamitous presence that haunts the seas and attacks ships. Most Umibōzu sightings begin on a calm night – then, out of nowhere, the waves begin to crash and the wind starts to blow. To the horror of Japanese sailors, the Umibōzu rises from the sea; however, due to its enormous size, they have only ever seen its head.

The Umibōzu will then sink the ship unless the sailors offer it a bottomless barrel. The creature tries to fill the barrel and use it to sink the ship but cannot understand why the barrel never fills. Amidst the Umibōzu’s confusion, the sailors have a chance to escape.

According to legend, the Umibōzu is the vengeful spirit of a drowned monk, now haunting the same villagers who once sacrificed monks to the sea.

Yamata-no-Orochi is one of the most physically imposing figures in Japanese mythology: its massive blue-black body is said to span over eight valleys and eight hills. Furthermore, it has blood-red eyes, eight heads, and eight tails.

The Yamata-no-Orochi once terrorized a family with eight daughters: every year, the great beast would come and devour one of the girls. The kami Susanoo was wandering the earth and came upon the family before their final daughter was set to be eaten by the Yamata-no-Orochi. Susanoo was able to trick the beast into drinking eight barrels of sake, until it became so intoxicated that it fell asleep. Susanoo then killed the beast, and in one of the tails of the great dragon, he found a sword named Kusanagi.

Settlers form the basis of your economy. They gather resources in a typical fashion and deposit them at upgradable Calpullis when they reach their carry capacity.

Make sure you have enough Settlers to maintain a steady flow of resources, but remember, they are weak in combat. Aztec Settlers can be expended to generate Favor through Devotion. To help the Aztecs keep pace with the expanding economies of other civilizations, Settlers are slightly cheaper than other villagers. The Chinampas Farm upgrade increases their Food production speed.

Quimichin Spies are agile scout units that can enter stealth within range of a treeline. But be careful. Other scout types and towers can see their silhouettes at a distance.

Warrior Priests are the common Aztec hero unit. They collect tonalli, dropped by defeated units, to supplement favour generation, and can construct religious buildings. They fight at close range and are especially strong against myth units given their Hero status, but they are also effective against human units.

Warrior Priests are necessary in any Aztec strategy, as they reduce reliance on the Teixiptla as the sole myth unit counter and contribute to Favor generation through tonalli absorption.

The Aztecs lack traditional cavalry, but Coyote Warriors help fill this role as swift infantry units that excel against ranged enemies.

Available early on, Coyote Warriors can become significantly more effective with the right upgrades and myth technologies. Specializing in them supports aggressive playstyles during the early and mid-game, but they begin to fall off in the late game, struggling against fortified positions and heavier enemy units.

Ocelotl Warriors were revered as elite Aztec fighters, embodying the fierce spirit and agility of the jaguar itself.

Ocelotl Warriors are versatile mid-game infantry known for their high damage, mobility, and stealth. Furthermore, they can leap at enemies, dealing bonus damage and on-hit effects.

Ocelotl Warriors automatically hide when close to trees, allowing them to excel at flanking. Ambushing opponents by leaping from stealth causes them to unleash a flurry of fast attacks as they take their opponents by surprise. But be careful. Scout types and towers can see their silhouettes at a distance.

Armed with spears and courage, Tlamanih carried out the will of the empire, often forming the first wave of any Aztec assault.

Tlamanih are fast, cost-effective spearmen who form the backbone of the Aztecs’ early military. Their mobility and early availability make them ideal for raids and early skirmishes.

In Aztec warfare, Eagle Warriors embodied both nobility and lethality; warriors who struck before the enemy could even prepare.

Eagle Warriors are powerful, mobile ranged generalists effective against most human units. With high attack range, speed, and mobility, they excel at kiting. Unlike more specialized units, they perform well without strict counter-matchup planning, and upgrades further boost their speed and damage.

Tequihua Archers are young warriors still proving themselves in battle, often given the role of harassing enemy lines with ranged attacks while the main force closed in.

Tequihua Archers are a cheap early ranged unit used to counter enemy infantry. To help them keep up with the Tlamanih's movements, they have above average mobility. Their attack range can also make them a decent defensive option when strategically positioned behind terrain or buildings.

Huitzilopochtli is the Aztec god of war, the sun, and conquest. He embodies martial strength and divine leadership, guiding the Aztecs through battle and expansion.

Each Major God can temporarily possess one Warrior Priest at a time as their Teixiptla, granting them immense power. The Teixiptla’s abilities and appearance depend on which Major God is being played. The Teixiptla deals significant damage with special attacks, making them a potent tool but also a prime target for enemies. As a Hero, the Teixiptla deals bonus damage to myth units and gains bonus stats with each Age.

After a short time, the Teixiptla’s mortal frame can no longer contain the power of the god possessing them, and the unit is lost. Players will have to choose when to invoke this power decisively.

Said to number four hundred, they represent the many different and unpredictable outcomes. Rather than symbols of pleasure alone, they reflect Aztec concerns about excess and imbalance.

Trade was vital to the strength and stability of the Aztec Empire. While the central valleys were rich in agricultural products, other goods, like obsidian, cacao, feathers, and cotton were imported from distant regions.

What makes this system remarkable is that it functioned without beasts of burden or wheeled transport. Human porters carried goods across vast distances, allowing trade networks to span much of Mesoamerica. Luxury items like cacao traveled hundreds of miles, demonstrating the efficiency and reach of Aztec trade.

Aztec merchants, known as Pochtecatl, traveled vast distances to exchange goods and gather intelligence. Markets, such as Tlatelolco, bustled with activity, drawing thousands of traders daily. Trade not only sustained the empire’s economy but also helped extend its influence far beyond the Valley of Mexico.

This large movable tower mounted stone throwers and ballistae of different sizes, with the smallest at the top. Two hundred men pushed the tower up to the enemy walls using parallel beams extending out from its bottom. The larger weapons in the machine battered the walls while the smaller ones swept defenders off the walls in preparation for an assault.

When the ram knocked the wall down, the attacking army could enter the city.

Although the men holding the ram were at great risk, this weapon could be put into action within hours of laying a siege. Portable rams were particularly effective in surprise attacks and against weak fortifications. They were popular among raiding armies and forces that could not linger outside of a city for a protracted siege.

The missile was usually a large metal, or metal-headed, bolt. Fired into a mass of men at ranges up to 1,000 feet, bolts could disable several enemies. Ballistas could be mounted on walls or ships, or wheeled out for battlefield use. They were not particularly effective against fortified buildings or walls.

Historical evidence suggests that these siege engines were used well into the 12th century.

The trireme (trieres in Greek) was named because the oarsmen were stationed in 3 rows, allowing more men to fit on a smaller ship. A standard trireme was about 120 ft long, and manned by over 150 oarsmen. The ships could cover about 160 nautical miles at a constant speed of 7.5 knots. They also had square sails, which could not always be used on the temperamental Mediterranean Sea. During the wars with Persia, Athens alone commanded over 200 of these ships.

Like many Egyptian ships, these vessels could be sailed down the Nile and rowed back the other direction. A set of 18 oars gave Egyptian warships good maneuverability, particularly over the non-rowed warships of their adversaries, such as the 'Sea Peoples'. Egyptian warships were equipped with rams, but combat typically consisted of boarding or missile fire. Egyptian ships had high bulwarks to protect against enemy missiles, and their own archers were trained in naval combat.

historia: Scandinavia had a long history of naval trading, which eventually developed into coastal raiding during the Viking Age. The longboat was a fast warship about 80 feet long, which could either be rowed or sailed from a single mast with a square sail. Maneuverability, high speed, and shallow draught allowed the ships to penetrate rivers, which the vikings used to attack even inland towns. While bulkier vessels could only be moored in a harbor, longboats could be beached right on the shore. Flexible hulls also allowed longboats to traverse the treacherous waves of the North Atlantic, despite being loaded down with goods and warriors. Viking chieftains were sometimes even buried in their ships.

historia: Junkozosen were rudimentary, semi-structured boats used in ancient Japan. A step above dugout canoes, Junkozosen had added side planks to improve stability in ocean waters. Scholars agree that the transition from dugout canoes to Junkozosen was a direct response to the rise in maritime trade – as inter-regional trade became more frequent in medieval Japan, the need for advances in shipbuilding grew. In addition to trade, Junkozosen were also used for fishing. They were typically constructed from cedar or cypress trees. This semi-structured boat represents a transitional period between simple canoes and fully structured plank ships.

Fishing tools included nets, lines with bone hooks, and spears. These canoes were used in lakes like Texcoco and Xochimilco to catch fish, shrimp, axolotls, and insect larvae. Though simple, they played a vital role in food supply, trade, and tribute in the Aztec Empire.

Arrow Canoes are narrow, maneuverable vessels manned by skilled warriors, equipped with ranged weapons, such as bows and slings. Fashioned from hollowed-out logs or built with planks, they have a flat bottom for stability in shallow waters and are paddle-powered by several men.

Arrow canoes allow quick troop movements, surprise attacks, and amphibious assaults, playing a key role in Aztec military strategy.

historia:
An Aztec transport ship was a large wooden canoe, used to move goods and people across the lakes and canals. These canoes were dugouts or plank-built, flat-bottomed, and paddle-powered, ideal for the shallow waters.

They carried food, building materials, tribute goods and market supplies. They also served as transport for soldiers or messengers. These canoes formed the backbone of the Aztec logistics and trade system across the empire’s vast network of waterways.
